asset.title: Interpreting narrative perspective: competing accounts of a fictional community archive exhibition
learning_objectives: Identify what the curator's first-person plural account explicitly states about the exhibition opening and distinguish those statements from inferences.
Locate specific omissions in the account and explain what those gaps do and do not permit a reader to conclude.
Explain why a situated first-person viewpoint does not by itself give access to other participants' motives.
Evaluate two defensible readings of the collective 'we' and state the limits of the claim made.
Distinguish what the volunteer explicitly reports from what a reader infers, using the wording of the passage.
Identify textual details that can support a reading of tentative belonging and details that can support unresolved exclusion.
Explain why co-present details (applause plus a withheld letter) do not by themselves establish censorship, motive, or content.
Compare a public collective framing with a private, situated hesitation and judge whether the accounts conflict or can coexist.
State the limits of one's own interpretation and name a plausible competing reading.

sections.heading: Question 1 · Supporting material
sections.text:
Source A: the curator's account (fictional, AI-authored teaching passage)

"We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history." The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition and is fictional. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

---

Source B: teaching note on perspective and interpretive limits (AI-authored)

A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim; different interpretations can meet these standards without agreeing on a single hidden intention.

sections.heading: Question 2 · Supporting material
sections.text:
Sources (all fictional, AI-authored for this exercise)

Source A — curator's account: "We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history." The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

Source B — volunteer's account: "I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it." The narrator reports gratitude and hesitation but does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

Source C — teaching note: A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission, or contrast. The curator's collective "we" can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.

---

Task conventions

Sources A and B are fictional teaching passages, not real interviews, real volunteers, or archival records; treat their narrators as constructed voices. Base every claim on wording inside Sources A and B, and apply Source C only as an interpretive rule, not as evidence about what happened at the exhibition. Do not import outside history, biography, or literary theory. Do not assume any motive, dissent, rejection, or exclusion that the passages do not state. Cite the source you draw each point from.

expected_steps: List the curator's explicit statements and specify the actions the collective 'we' covers.
Name at least one specific omission (photograph selection, rejected contributions, visitor reactions) and explain what it prevents knowing.
Apply the statement/inference distinction to show a situated viewpoint is not automatic access to other participants' motives.
Present both readings of 'we' — aspiration to shared ownership and unstated internal differences — and judge or explain their relative support with wording from the passage.
State what the passage does not establish about harmony, exclusion, or hidden intentions.
Keep the method note's stray details (applause, unopened letter) out of the evidence about the exhibition.

questions.stem:
Write a short analysis (roughly 200–300 words) of the curator's account in Source A, using Source B for interpretive principles. Address all of the following in order, and refer to specific wording from the passage:

(a) List what the curator explicitly states about the opening and identify the basis of the collective 'we' (what actions does 'we' actually cover?).
(b) Name at least one specific omission in the account and explain what that gap prevents a reader from knowing.
(c) Explain why a first-person account can convey a situated viewpoint without granting automatic knowledge of other participants' motives. Use at least one of the passage's details to show the difference between a statement and an inference.
(d) Present two readings of the collective 'we' — one as an aspiration to shared ownership, one as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated — and judge which the passage better supports, or explain why both remain defensible. Support your judgment with wording from the passage.
(e) State clearly what the passage does not establish about group harmony, exclusion, or hidden intentions.

Note on evidence discipline: Source B mentions a volunteer's applause and an unopened letter, but neither appears in Source A. Do not use them as evidence about what happened at the exhibition, and do not assume any motive, dissent, or exclusion that the passage does not state.
questions.answer:
A defensible response can look like this (other readings are acceptable if they meet the same criteria):

(a) Explicit statements: the exhibition was finally opened 'together'; volunteers carried boxes from their homes; children stopped before the wall of photographs; captions were chosen 'short enough to read in a crowded room'; the opening 'felt like a beginning, not a finished history.' The 'we' covers the opening ('We finally opened') and the caption choice ('We chose captions'). Its grammatical basis is therefore joint action at the opening, not documented agreement among all contributors about selection, content, or purpose.

(b) Omission: the account never says who selected the photographs; it also does not list rejected contributions or report every visitor's reaction. These gaps mean a reader cannot know how selection decisions were made, whose material was left out, or how visitors other than the children who stopped (and whose reaction is not described in words) responded. The children's stopping is an observed action, not a report of their view of the exhibition.

(c) Because the account is first-person, it delivers one situated viewpoint — what this narrator saw, did, and felt ('felt like a beginning'). It does not follow that the narrator knows what volunteers or children thought. Example: 'Volunteers carried boxes' is a statement about visible action; 'the volunteers wanted the archive to represent everyone' would be an inference, unsupported by the passage.

(d) Reading 1 (aspiration to shared ownership): 'We finally opened the exhibition together,' volunteers bringing boxes from their homes, and a caption policy designed for a crowded room all suggest an effort to make the event collective and publicly readable. Reading 2 (unstated differences): the 'we' is asserted by a single narrator; no other participant speaks in the passage, and the account acknowledges only an unfinished process ('not a finished history'), so disagreement, unequal labour, or contested choices would not appear even if present. This second reading is well supported because the narration supplies only one voice and one viewpoint; the first is also supported but rests on the narrator's framing. Both can be defended, provided the writer cites wording and concedes the competing reading.

(e) Limits: the passage does not establish that the group was harmonious or unanimous, that anyone was excluded or censored, or what any participant intended. Claims of censorship, hidden agendas, or unresolved exclusion go beyond what the text states.
questions.explanation: Strong answers do five things: (1) separate explicit statements (opening, boxes, children stopping, short captions, 'a beginning, not a finished history') from inferences; (2) name a concrete omission — photograph selection, rejected contributions, visitor reactions — and say what it blocks; (3) apply the statement/inference distinction to show that a first-person account is situated rather than omniscient; (4) argue for or against the shared-ownership reading of 'we' while acknowledging the alternative; and (5) mark the limits, refusing to claim harmony, exclusion, censorship, or hidden intentions that the text never asserts. Answers that offer a different but text-supported judgment on the 'we' still meet the criteria if they cite wording from the passage and concede the competing reading.
questions.difficulty_reason: The task requires coordinating two sources and five constraints: extracting explicit statements, identifying what omissions block, distinguishing a situated viewpoint from omniscience, weighing two competing readings of 'we' with textual support, and refusing conclusions the passage does not license (including ignoring details that appear only in the teaching note). It cannot be completed by restating a definition of narrative perspective; it demands judgment about evidence and stated limits.

expected_steps: Sort the volunteer's explicit reports from inferences, quoting specific wording for the photograph, caption, applause, and letter.
Pair one belonging detail with one exclusion detail and explain what each can and cannot support.
Explain why applause plus a withheld letter shows neither censorship nor the letter's content or motive.
Compare the curator's collective framing with the volunteer's private hesitation and judge conflict versus coexistence using both passages.
Offer one overall reading, name a plausible rival, and state the limits of the claim.
Name at least one assertion the text blocks and cite the wording that blocks it.

questions.stem:
Write a short analysis (roughly 250–350 words) of the volunteer's account in Source B, using Source C's interpretive rules and Source A for comparison. Ground every claim in specific wording, cite the source for each point, and address all of the following in order:

(a) State what the volunteer explicitly reports about (i) the photograph and the caption, (ii) the applause, and (iii) the letter. Separate these reports from anything you only infer.
(b) Select one detail that could support a reading of tentative belonging and one detail that could support a reading of unresolved exclusion.
(c) Explain why the applause together with the letter kept in the bag does not establish censorship, and does not tell a reader what the letter contained or why it was withheld.
(d) Compare the curator's public framing in Source A with the volunteer's private hesitation in Source B, and judge whether the two accounts conflict or can coexist. Justify your judgment with wording from both passages.
(e) Offer one defensible overall reading of the volunteer's perspective; name a plausible competing reading; state the limits of your own claim.
(f) Identify at least one thing your reading must not assert (for example, about the letter's contents, a rejection, or hidden motives) and explain what in the text blocks that assertion.

Evidence discipline: do not invent the letter's contents, a reason for withholding it, or any rejection of it; do not treat Source C as evidence about the exhibition; do not use outside history or theory.
questions.answer:
Reference response (one defensible reading; other evidence-grounded readings may also satisfy the criteria).

(a) Explicit reports only (Source B): the volunteer recognized "my father's coat in a photograph," while "the caption named only the factory"; the volunteer "was glad that someone had kept the picture"; "When the curator thanked us, I applauded"; "I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag"; "Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it." The passage states gratitude and hesitation but not a cause; it does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

(b) Tentative belonging: applauding the curator's thanks, being glad the picture was kept, and leaving open "another occasion" all show continuing, if conditional, participation. Unresolved exclusion: the caption names the factory but not the person the volunteer recognizes in the coat, and a personal document stays in the bag while the public thanks are applauded.

(c) The applause and the bagged letter are co-present, not causally linked by the narrator. Nothing in Source B says anyone refused the letter, and the volunteer supplies no reason. Source C states the text "does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents." Attributing the withholding to rejection, fear, or anything else means adding a cause the passage never gives.

(d) They can coexist. Source A's "We finally opened the exhibition together" and "a beginning, not a finished history" frame the event publicly as collective and unfinished; Source B does not contradict that frame—the volunteer applauds and values the picture—but supplies a private interior the curator's account does not report. Source C notes a first-person account gives "a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives," so the curator's "we" need not be read as a claim that everyone felt fully included. Conflict arises only if "together" is over-read as a report of unanimous feeling, which Source A does not state.

(e) Defensible reading: tentative belonging—glad participation and public affirmation, alongside something personal held back with the door left open ("Perhaps"). Competing reading: unresolved exclusion, resting on the caption that names the factory rather than the person in the coat, and on the letter staying in the bag. A mixed reading is also defensible. Limits: the text does not say the caption omission caused the withholding, does not identify the letter's contents, and does not report any rejection, so neither reading may claim to know the volunteer's reasons.

(f) The reading must not assert (i) what the letter contained, (ii) that it was rejected or censored, or (iii) that exclusion explains the withholding. Source B explicitly reports none of these—"does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained"—and Source C confirms the text "does not establish censorship."
questions.explanation: Scoring points: (1) reports only what Source B states, without adding causes or contents; (2) names a belonging detail and an exclusion detail, each tied to wording; (3) explains the gap between co-presence and causation for applause plus the withheld letter; (4) judges conflict vs. coexistence using both accounts and the situated-viewpoint rule; (5) gives one reading, names a rival, and states limits; (6) names at least one forbidden assertion and the textual evidence that blocks it. Strong answers quote or closely paraphrase, cite sources, and mark inferences as inferences. Accept any overall reading—belonging, exclusion, or mixture—that meets these criteria and keeps the letter's contents, motive, and any rejection unspecified.
questions.difficulty_reason: Hard because it requires integrating three sources, weighing details that pull in opposite directions, distinguishing explicit statement from inference, judging whether two accounts conflict, and stating the limits of one's own reading—while resisting the temptation to invent the letter's contents, a motive, or a rejection. Recalling what the passage says is necessary but not sufficient.
